step4.objective:
• Installed flow entries retained without expiry for the whole period the controller connection is interrupted when the non-rule-expiry option is in effect.
  • Traffic matching retained flow entries forwarded or blocked exactly as before for the duration of the interruption.
  • Traffic matching no installed entry handled according to the secure fail mode while the controller is unreachable.
  • Flow entries subject to normal timeout expiry during an interruption when the non-rule-expiry option is absent, as the default behaviour.
  • The flow table resynchronised with the controller on reconnection, with stale entries replaced and no duplicate or orphaned entries.
  • Retained entries remaining intact across repeated short interruptions, with no gradual loss of entries.
  • Removal of the non-rule-expiry option restoring default expiry behaviour on the next interruption.
  • An incompatible fail-mode and non-rule-expiry combination rejected with a clear error, with the prior OpenFlow configuration retained.
  • The fail mode and non-rule-expiry option reported in the OpenFlow status and persisting across a save and reload.

steps.description: Note: Related ART Tests linked in Traceability.

Verify flow retention with the DUT connected to an OpenFlow controller, the non-rule-expiry option enabled, and a set of flow entries installed that carry both idle and hard timeouts. Interrupt the controller connection for longer than the shortest installed timeout and confirm the installed entries remain present throughout the interruption.

With the non-rule-expiry option enabled and a traffic generator attached to the DUT data ports, install entries that forward and entries that drop matching traffic. Run traffic matching each entry before, during and after a controller interruption and confirm the forwarding and blocking behaviour is unchanged while the controller is unreachable.

During a controller interruption with the secure fail mode in effect, send traffic that matches no installed entry alongside traffic that matches retained entries. Confirm the unmatched traffic is handled according to the secure fail mode and is not forwarded through any other path.

Repeat the interruption with the non-rule-expiry option absent, using entries whose timeouts elapse within the interruption period. Confirm the entries expire on their normal timeouts and that traffic previously matching them is then handled as unmatched traffic.

While the controller is disconnected, change the controller's intended flow set by modifying, adding and removing entries. Restore the connection and confirm the DUT flow table resynchronises to the controller's view, with stale entries replaced and no duplicate or orphaned entries remaining.

With the non-rule-expiry option enabled and a populated flow table, interrupt and restore the controller connection repeatedly with short interruptions, including interruptions shorter than the controller's reconnection interval. Confirm the flow entry count and content stay intact after every cycle, with no gradual loss of entries.

Remove the non-rule-expiry option from a DUT that previously had it enabled, with timed entries installed. Interrupt the controller connection again and confirm the entries now expire on their normal timeouts as with the default behaviour.

Attempt to configure the non-rule-expiry option together with a fail mode it is not compatible with, both by adding the option to an existing fail mode and by changing the fail mode while the option is set. Confirm each attempt is rejected with a clear error and the previous OpenFlow configuration is retained.

Verify the fail mode and non-rule-expiry option are reported in the OpenFlow status for both the enabled and default configurations. Save the configuration, reload the DUT, and confirm both settings persist and that retention behaviour on the next interruption matches the saved configuration.

During a controller interruption with the secure fail mode in effect, send traffic that matches no installed entry alongside traffic that matches retained entries. Confirm the unmatched traffic is handled according to the secure fail mode and is not forwarded through any other path.

Repeat the interruption with the non-rule-expiry option absent, using entries whose timeouts elapse within the interruption period. Confirm the entries expire on their normal timeouts and that traffic previously matching them is then handled as unmatched traffic.

While the controller is disconnected, change the controller's intended flow set by modifying, adding and removing entries. Restore the connection and confirm the DUT flow table resynchronises to the controller's view, with stale entries replaced and no duplicate or orphaned entries remaining.

With the non-rule-expiry option enabled and a populated flow table, interrupt and restore the controller connection repeatedly with short interruptions, including interruptions shorter than the controller's reconnection interval. Confirm the flow entry count and content stay intact after every cycle, with no gradual loss of entries.

Remove the non-rule-expiry option from a DUT that previously had it enabled, with timed entries installed. Interrupt the controller connection again and confirm the entries now expire on their normal timeouts as with the default behaviour.

Attempt to configure the non-rule-expiry option together with a fail mode it is not compatible with, both by adding the option to an existing fail mode and by changing the fail mode while the option is set. Confirm each attempt is rejected with a clear error and the previous OpenFlow configuration is retained.

Verify the fail mode and non-rule-expiry option are reported in the OpenFlow status for both the enabled and default configurations. Save the configuration, reload the DUT, and confirm both settings persist and that retention behaviour on the next interruption matches the saved configuration.

provenance.steps_prompt:
You are drafting Zephyr-ready verification steps for a manual test case. The objective below is finalized (user-reviewed). Derive the steps from it. An objective bullet states an END STATE — what should be true. A step is a PROCEDURE — what someone does, and under what conditions. A step must add test-design information the bullet does not already carry: the setup, the data, the variation, the thing being exercised. Re-wording a bullet adds nothing and is not a step — whatever verb it opens with. "Verify …" is a perfectly good way to begin a real step and many steps here should use it; the fault is restatement, never the word. ## Case AWPTCM-T44333 — OpenFlow conn interruption non-rule-expired ## Finalized objective (authoritative)
  • Installed flow entries retained without expiry for the whole period the controller connection is interrupted when the non-rule-expiry option is in effect.
  • Traffic matching retained flow entries forwarded or blocked exactly as before for the duration of the interruption.
  • Traffic matching no installed entry handled according to the secure fail mode while the controller is unreachable.
  • Flow entries subject to normal timeout expiry during an interruption when the non-rule-expiry option is absent, as the default behaviour.
  • The flow table resynchronised with the controller on reconnection, with stale entries replaced and no duplicate or orphaned entries.
  • Retained entries remaining intact across repeated short interruptions, with no gradual loss of entries.
  • Removal of the non-rule-expiry option restoring default expiry behaviour on the next interruption.
  • An incompatible fail-mode and non-rule-expiry combination rejected with a clear error, with the prior OpenFlow configuration retained.
  • The fail mode and non-rule-expiry option reported in the OpenFlow status and persisting across a save and reload.
## Rules - The FIRST step is injected server-side as a traceability note — DO NOT generate it. - Generate ONLY the subsequent verification steps exercising the objective's artefacts. - Cover each major objective bullet: positive, negative, special conditions, reporting. - Keep each step high-level enough to be reusable across platforms, but specific enough to be testable. Naming exact values, counts and timings is the PyTest script's job, not this one — a manual step that dictates them narrows the tester to one way of exercising the feature instead of leaving them to produce evidence that it works. - LEAVE `expectedResult` EMPTY on every step. This is deliberate, not an omission. The tester reads the objective and the step and reasons out what should happen; stating the outcome narrows them to producing exactly that result instead of evidence that the feature works. The objective already carries the expected outcomes. - Say WHAT is being exercised, not which command to type. Proving the step was taken — capturing `show` output as evidence — is the generated PyTest script's job, and naming commands or device registers here invents mechanisms that may not exist and narrows the tester besides. - Where a step depends on topology, say which roles it needs (e.g. two links between the DUT and a partner), never a device model or a port number. - Platform-agnostic language: no product names, no hardcoded port strings. ## Output format — this example IS the specification; match its level of detail [ { "description": "Verify LLDP operation with the DUT and its link partner both running default timers. Confirm neighbours are discovered on the test link and that each side reports the other's chassis and port identity.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Vary the transmit interval and hold multiplier across their supported range, including the minimum and maximum. Confirm advertisements are sent at the configured rate and that the neighbour's advertised lifetime tracks the configured values.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Set the transmit interval below the supported minimum and above the supported maximum. Confirm the DUT rejects both and retains its previous configuration.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Disable LLDP transmit on the DUT while leaving receive enabled, then re-enable it. Confirm the neighbour ages out and is rediscovered, and that the port reports the change.", "expectedResult": "" } ] Output the JSON array ONLY. No prose, no markdown fence.

gaps: No ART automated tests were selected as related coverage for AWPTCM-T44333, so automation does not currently address the OpenFlow connection-interruption behaviour tied to AWP-29525 (mapped with medium confidence). No confirmed TestLink artefacts or Zephyr cross-references are available either, so this gap cannot be offset or clarified by historical intent. The main uncovered behaviours are controller connection loss and recovery where flow entries are not removed by rule expiry (idle/hard timeout), including whether those entries persist through the interruption. Also uncovered are fail-mode handling during the outage, re-synchronisation of flow state after reconnection, and observability of connection-state transitions and flow-table consistency. Edge cases such as repeated or prolonged interruptions, and interruptions that coincide with flow modifications, also lack automated validation and remain dependent on manual execution.

  • Installed flow entries retained without expiry for the whole period the controller connection is interrupted when the non-rule-expiry option is in effect.
  • Traffic matching retained flow entries forwarded or blocked exactly as before for the duration of the interruption.
  • Traffic matching no installed entry handled according to the secure fail mode while the controller is unreachable.
  • Flow entries subject to normal timeout expiry during an interruption when the non-rule-expiry option is absent, as the default behaviour.
  • The flow table resynchronised with the controller on reconnection, with stale entries replaced and no duplicate or orphaned entries.
  • Retained entries remaining intact across repeated short interruptions, with no gradual loss of entries.
  • Removal of the non-rule-expiry option restoring default expiry behaviour on the next interruption.
  • An incompatible fail-mode and non-rule-expiry combination rejected with a clear error, with the prior OpenFlow configuration retained.
  • The fail mode and non-rule-expiry option reported in the OpenFlow status and persisting across a save and reload.
## Rules - The FIRST step is injected server-side as a traceability note — DO NOT generate it. - Generate ONLY the subsequent verification steps exercising the objective's artefacts. - Cover each major objective bullet: positive, negative, special conditions, reporting. - Keep each step high-level enough to be reusable across platforms, but specific enough to be testable. Naming exact values, counts and timings is the PyTest script's job, not this one — a manual step that dictates them narrows the tester to one way of exercising the feature instead of leaving them to produce evidence that it works. - LEAVE `expectedResult` EMPTY on every step. This is deliberate, not an omission. The tester reads the objective and the step and reasons out what should happen; stating the outcome narrows them to producing exactly that result instead of evidence that the feature works. The objective already carries the expected outcomes. - Say WHAT is being exercised, not which command to type. Proving the step was taken — capturing `show` output as evidence — is the generated PyTest script's job, and naming commands or device registers here invents mechanisms that may not exist and narrows the tester besides. - Where a step depends on topology, say which roles it needs (e.g. two links between the DUT and a partner), never a device model or a port number. - Platform-agnostic language: no product names, no hardcoded port strings. ## Output format — this example IS the specification; match its level of detail [ { "description": "Verify LLDP operation with the DUT and its link partner both running default timers. Confirm neighbours are discovered on the test link and that each side reports the other's chassis and port identity.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Vary the transmit interval and hold multiplier across their supported range, including the minimum and maximum. Confirm advertisements are sent at the configured rate and that the neighbour's advertised lifetime tracks the configured values.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Set the transmit interval below the supported minimum and above the supported maximum. Confirm the DUT rejects both and retains its previous configuration.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Disable LLDP transmit on the DUT while leaving receive enabled, then re-enable it. Confirm the neighbour ages out and is rediscovered, and that the port reports the change.", "expectedResult": "" } ] Output the JSON array ONLY. No prose, no markdown fence.
